title: YOU’RE TIRED OF DOING GOOD—AND GOD KNEW THIS MOMENT WOULD COME
paragraphs: YOU’RE TIRED OF DOING GOOD—AND GOD KNEW THIS MOMENT WOULD COME
The deeper meaning of Galatians 6:9 is not “try harder.” It is a breathtaking promise for exhausted believers who have been faithful so long that quitting has started to feel reasonable.
There is a kind of tiredness sleep cannot fix.
You can sleep eight hours and still wake up carrying it.
You can worship with everyone else while carrying it.
You can smile at church while carrying it.
You can tell people, “God is good,” and believe every word of it… while privately wondering how much longer you can keep doing what is right when doing right does not seem to be changing anything.
You prayed.
Nothing moved.
You forgave.
They hurt you again.
You served.
Nobody noticed.
You gave.
Nobody thanked you.
You resisted the temptation.
The temptation returned.
You tried to raise your children in the Lord, but you are watching one of them wander.
You kept showing up for your marriage while wondering whether the other person even sees the sacrifice.
You tried to live with integrity while watching people who compromised seemingly get ahead.
You have been asking God for restoration, healing, direction, breakthrough, reconciliation, provision…
and somewhere between the first prayer and the hundredth prayer, something inside you became tired.
Not necessarily rebellious.
Not necessarily unbelieving.
Just tired.
And perhaps that is why Galatians 6:9 can sound completely different when you read what Paul actually wrote.
The Greek text says:
Τὸ δὲ καλὸν ποιοῦντες μὴ ἐγκακῶμεν, καιρῷ γὰρ ἰδίῳ θερίσομεν μὴ ἐκλυόμενοι.
To de kalon poiountes mē enkakōmen, kairō gar idiō therisomen mē eklyomenoi.
A faithful rendering is:
“And let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.”
Do not rush past those words.
Paul was not speaking to people who had never started doing good.
He was speaking to people who were already doing it.
That changes everything.
The danger in Galatians 6:9 is not merely refusing to begin.
The danger is becoming exhausted after beginning well.
The Greek verb translated “grow weary,” ἐγκακέω — enkakeō, carries the idea of losing heart, becoming discouraged, or becoming weary in doing what is right.
Paul understands something painfully human:
You can love Jesus and become tired.
You can obey God and become discouraged.
You can know the truth and still feel the emotional weight of waiting.
You can plant faithfully and become frustrated because the ground above the seed still looks empty.
And God does not shame the exhausted believer here.
He speaks to the exhausted believer.
“Do not lose heart.”
Because there is something underneath the soil that you cannot see.
Galatians 6 is filled with the language of sowing and reaping.
Just before verse 9, Paul writes:
Then he contrasts sowing to the flesh with sowing to the Spirit.
“For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.” — Galatians 6:8
Then comes the sentence for the person who is exhausted from planting seeds that appear to be doing nothing:
Do not become weary.
You will reap.
But notice what Scripture does not promise.
Paul does not promise that every earthly dream will eventually happen if you simply refuse to quit.
Galatians 6:9 is not a blank cheque for whatever outcome we desire.
It does not mean every business will succeed.
It does not mean every relationship will be restored.
It does not mean every illness will disappear in this life.
It does not mean God owes us the specific harvest we imagined.
The context is much richer than motivational optimism.
Paul is talking about a life being sown toward the Spirit.
Faithfulness.
Holiness.
Generosity.
Love.
Bearing one another’s burdens.
Doing good.
Persevering in Christ.
Living in the reality of the new creation.
This is not “believe in yourself until your dreams come true.”
This is:
Keep trusting Christ when obedience becomes expensive.
There is another word in the Greek that deserves your attention.
καιρῷ — kairō.
“Season.”
Paul says:
καιρῷ γὰρ ἰδίῳ θερίσομεν
“For in its own season we will reap.”
Not necessarily your preferred season.
Not the season your impatience demanded.
Not according to the deadline you secretly gave God.
The appointed season.
And this is where waiting becomes painful.
Because sowing and reaping happen in different seasons.
You can plant in tears and see nothing for a while.
You can pray for someone who appears to be moving farther from God.
You can choose purity while loneliness whispers that compromise would be easier.
You can forgive while part of you desperately wants revenge.
You can serve quietly while someone louder receives the applause.
You can give generously when nobody knows what the gift cost you.
You can open your Bible while spiritually numb and read because you know you need truth more than another distraction.
You can whisper the name “Jesus” through tears when you have no impressive prayer left.
And none of those seeds are invisible to God.
The world trains us to expect immediate feedback.
Post something.
Check the reaction.
Send something.
Wait for the reply.
Work.
Expect the reward.
Invest.
Measure the return.
But the kingdom of God repeatedly teaches us how to live between seed and harvest.
That space can be brutal.
Because after you put the seed into the ground, it disappears.
Think about that.
The farmer takes something valuable from his hand and intentionally buries it.
For a while, the evidence seems to suggest that he has lost it.
The soil does not applaud.
The field does not immediately explain what is happening underneath.
The farmer has to trust a process he cannot watch.
Maybe that describes where you are.
You have been faithful…
and all you can see is dirt.
You prayed for your child…
dirt.
You resisted the old addiction today…
dirt.
You chose not to send the message your anger wanted to send…
dirt.
You apologized even though your pride screamed against it…
dirt.
You opened Scripture instead of returning to the thing that keeps poisoning you…
dirt.
You gave somebody another chance…
dirt.
You kept serving…
dirt.
You kept believing…
dirt.
And because nothing appears to be growing, the enemy whispers:
“See? It was pointless.”
But buried is not the same as dead.
Hidden is not the same as forgotten.
And waiting is not proof that God has abandoned you.
The seed does not need applause to germinate.
Neither does obedience.
Some of the holiest moments of your life may be moments nobody ever sees.
Jesus taught His disciples about a Father who sees what is done in secret.
Your Father sees.
That matters when nobody else does.
But Galatians 6:9 contains a condition we cannot sentimentalize:
μὴ ἐκλυόμενοι — mē eklyomenoi
“if we do not give up,” or more literally, if we do not become exhausted to the point of collapsing or loosening our hold.
There comes a moment when weariness begins negotiating with conviction.
Maybe just this once.
Maybe holiness is not worth it.
Maybe prayer does not matter.
Maybe forgiveness was foolish.
Maybe nobody would know.
Maybe I can return to the person I used to be.
Maybe I should stop trying.
That is precisely where this verse meets us.
Not on a motivational poster.
In the private war.
The moment your flesh offers you an easier road.
The moment obedience feels unbearably slow.
The moment compromise promises immediate relief.
Paul says:
Do not surrender the field simply because harvest has not arrived yet.
But there is an even deeper truth.
Christian perseverance is not ultimately a story about how strong you are.
It is about Christ.
Paul had already made the center of Galatians unmistakable:
“I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.” — Galatians 2:20
The Christian life is not you gritting your teeth until heaven.
Jesus is not standing at the finish line shouting, “Try harder!”
He is the crucified and risen Savior upon whom your entire hope depends.
Your salvation was never purchased by your ability to persevere perfectly.
It was purchased by His blood.
You will stumble.
You will become tired.
There may even be moments when you fall terribly.
Peter knew that.
He promised Jesus loyalty and then denied knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing your own voice say you do not know the One you love.
Imagine looking back over a failure and thinking:
After everything Jesus has done for me…
how could I?
Yet Peter’s scandal was not the final chapter.
Jesus met him again.
Jesus restored him.
Jesus recommissioned him.
Grace rewrote what shame wanted to make permanent.
That does not make sin harmless.
Grace never calls darkness light.
Grace brings us into the light.
Grace says, “Repent. Come home. There is still mercy at the feet of Jesus.”
Maybe your weariness is not merely from doing good.
Maybe you are tired because you have been hiding.
Tired from maintaining appearances.
Tired from telling everyone you are okay.
Tired from carrying a secret habit.
Tired from promising God, “Never again,” and then returning to it.
Tired from shame.
Listen carefully.
Galatians does not point exhausted sinners toward self-salvation.
It points us toward Jesus Christ.
The answer to your sin is not pretending harder.
Repent.
Bring it into the light.
Confess.
Run toward Christ instead of away from Him.
The cross is proof that your sin is more serious than modern culture wants you to believe…
and that the mercy of God in Christ is more astonishing than your shame wants you to believe.
Jesus did not die because humanity needed inspiration.
He died because sinners needed redemption.
He rose because death would not have the final word.
And everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith discovers something scandalous:
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
That is why “do not grow weary” cannot mean “pretend you are never tired.”
Sometimes perseverance looks like crying while praying.
Sometimes it looks like asking another believer for help.
Sometimes it looks like confessing what you have hidden.
Sometimes it looks like deleting the number.
Closing the browser.
Walking away.
Making the call.
Opening the Bible again.
Returning to church.
Forgiving again.
Getting on your knees again.
Whispering, “Jesus, help me,” because those are the only three words you can manage.
Sometimes faithfulness is not dramatic.
Sometimes it is simply refusing to make a permanent decision during a temporary season of exhaustion.
You do not have to see the harvest today to remain faithful today.
That may be the word somebody reading this desperately needed.
You keep asking God to show you the entire field.
Maybe He is asking you to trust Him with the next seed.
Today.
Not ten years from now.
Today.
Do the next faithful thing.
Love the person in front of you.
Tell the truth.
Resist the temptation.
Forgive.
Repent.
Pray.
Serve.
Give.
Encourage somebody.
Open Scripture.
Return to Christ.
Keep sowing to the Spirit.
And when you are weak, remember that the Gospel has never been the story of impressive people proving themselves worthy of God.
It is the story of sinners rescued by a worthy Savior.
Be honest.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting, “I need Christ, and I am refusing to walk away,” becomes the beginning of an honest conversation with believers who have been fighting battles of their own.
Pray for them.
We were never meant to carry every burden alone.
Sharing Christian content does not earn favor with God. Jesus Christ alone saves, entirely by grace.
But if Gospel-centered truth has strengthened you, supporting its continued spread can be one practical way of participating in getting that truth in front of another weary person.
If this ministry is feeding your faith, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has stopped attending church.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person quietly battling addiction.
Invite the seeker with more questions than answers.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending to have everything together.
Let them encounter the real Gospel:
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Repentance matters.
But mercy is real.
The cross is real.
The tomb is empty.
Forgiveness is available.
And Jesus Christ still transforms sinners.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
And comment.
Tell us where you are in the field.
Are you planting?
Waiting?
Weeping?
Returning?
Trying not to quit?
If words are difficult, simply write:
Because somewhere else, another exhausted believer may read your words and realize they are not the only person struggling to remain faithful.
Galatians 6:9 does not promise an easy field.
It promises that faithfulness in Christ is not meaningless.
So when tomorrow comes and the soil still looks unchanged…
plant again.
When nobody applauds…
plant again.
When temptation returns…
look to Christ and plant again.
When shame tells you that your failure has disqualified you…
repent, receive His mercy, get up, and plant again.
When your heart whispers, “What if none of this matters?”…
remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that the God who sees the seed also knows the season.
You may be staring at an empty field tonight.
God sees every seed beneath it.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you after everything else fades is this:
Do not abandon in exhaustion what you entrusted to God in faith simply because the harvest is still underground.
